descript.abstract:
This dataset presents modeled values of dilation tendency and slip tendency for faults within and surrounding the Wilbur Springs region of northern California, including the Bartlett Springs Fault, Cross Springs Fault, Little Indian Valley Fault Zone, and a network of secondary structures. The region is actively deforming, as evidenced by ongoing uplift and folding, suggesting it is currently undergoing transpression and right-lateral shear in the larger San Andreas plate boundary.
Dilation and slip tendency describe the relative measure of how favorably oriented a fault is for slip under a given stress field, these are not probabilities although they are represented by values of 0 to 1. Dilation tendency is the tendency for faults to open in response to the regional stress field, while slip tendency represents the tendency that a fault will experience slip. Together, these measures provide insight into fault mechanics and potential fluid pathways under current stress conditions.
The stress field used in these calculations assumes a maximum horizontal compressive stress oriented N26°E, consistent with regional stress inversion studies (Provost and Houston, 2003). Relative stress magnitudes are derived from stress drop data within the broader San Andreas fault system (Lozos, 2015). These stress-based metrics were applied to detailed fault geometries in 10-meter long segments to assess spatial patterns of slip and dilation potential, which may be relevant to understanding seismic hazard and fluid migration in the area.
descript.purpose: This dataset was developed to characterize the mechanical behavior of faults in the Wilbur Springs region of northern California under present-day tectonic stress conditions. By quantifying spatial patterns of dilation tendency and slip tendency, this product supports ongoing research into fault slip behavior, stress-driven fluid migration, and seismic hazard assessment in Northern California. These results are intended for use by geoscientists, land and resource managers, and agencies involved in geothermal exploration, infrastructure planning, and natural hazard mitigation. The fine-scale fault modeling at 10-meter resolution provides a foundation for further investigations into the relationship between fault geometry, stress, and deformation processes in transpressional settings.

attracc.attraccr: Attribute accuracy is limited by the resolution of the original mapping (approximately 1:24,000 scale), potential digitization artifacts, and assumptions inherent in the stress model used for the calculations. All attributes were reviewed for logical consistency, and calculated values were screened for errors. Overall, the data are suitable for structural analysis and interpretation of fault-controlled fluid pathways or slip behavior under the modeled stress conditions.

dataqual.logic: Fault trace data were reviewed for logical consistency to ensure accurate representation and analysis. All attribute values, including strike, dilation tendency, and slip tendency, fall within expected geologic and computational ranges. The dataset was checked for omission and duplication of features; no unintended gaps or redundant fault segments were identified. Fault traces were segmented at 10-meter intervals or less if the length of the fault did not divide equally by 10.
dataqual.complete: This dataset includes fault traces, segment orientations, and modeled values of dilation tendency and slip tendency for faults located within the eastern portion of the northern California Coast Ranges, focused specifically along the southern part of the Bartlett Springs Fault Zone. The spatial extent of the dataset is limited to the area investigated and does not extend beyond the mapped region. No data are included for regions outside the study area, and the dataset should not be interpreted as a comprehensive inventory of all faults in the broader Coast Ranges. The dataset is limited in scope to derived fault segment attributes—strike, dilation tendency, and slip tendency—and does not include additional geologic context, fault names, or structural relationships beyond what was necessary for orientation-based stress modeling. All mapped segments were reviewed to ensure full coverage within the study extent, and no known omissions or gaps in the modeled fault data are present within the defined boundaries.

Orientation data from each segment were then input into a program to calculate dilation tendency and slip tendency.

overview.eaover:
These datasets contain fault segment geometries and associated slip and dilation tendency values for the southern Bartlett Springs Fault and adjacent fault zones in the Wilbur Springs area. Fault traces were segmented at 10-meter intervals to capture local variations in fault orientation for stress analysis. Each segment includes a calculated angle (CompassA) representing fault strike.
Using a simplified stress model, both slip tendency and dilation tendency were computed for each fault segment to evaluate how favorably oriented the faults are for slip or extensional opening under the regional stress field. Slip tendency reflects the ratio of resolved shear stress to normal stress on a fault plane and indicates the likelihood of fault slip, while dilation tendency quantifies the tendency of a fault segment to dilate or open in extension. Both metrics range from 0 (no tendency) to 1 (maximum tendency), and are spatially distributed along the fault network to highlight segments most likely to be critically stressed for slip or statically stressed open.
These data offer a structural framework for evaluating fault-controlled permeability and identifying zones of potential fluid pathways or induced seismicity in geothermal or tectonically active settings.
Slip and Dilation Tendency Calculations ---------------------------------------
Slip tendency (Ts) and dilation tendency (Td) were calculated for each fault segment using a simplified regional stress tensor.
Slip Tendency (Ts): Ts = τ / σₙ
Where: τ = shear stress on the fault plane σₙ = normal stress on the fault plane (positive in compression)
Ts values were normalized by the maximum value in the dataset.
Dilation Tendency (Td): Td = (σ₁ - σₙ) / (σ₁ - σ₃)
Where: σ₁ = maximum principal stress σ₃ = minimum principal stress σₙ = normal stress on the fault plane
Both Ts and Td range from 0 (no tendency) to 1 (maximum tendency).
